1.pericope_label: Samson sees a woman of Timnath, and it was of the Lord

schools.summary: Restrict the phrase to permission, since in no other sense can it be understood; refuse to let the reason she is right in my eyes pass as warrant for the random choice of a spouse, comparing the will that makes its own determinations its rule of right to the motto cast on the cannon of Louis the Fourteenth, that his will backed by instruments of destruction shall decide right and wrong; and supply the later history of the town.

Take the phrase to mean that God overruled events to his own ends, making the fierceness of men praise him, and cite the sense of divine rule found even in Homer; warn that some make Jehovah the seeker of the quarrel, which is unlikely; state the law exactly, since only Canaanite marriages are expressly forbidden, so that the parents' aversion rests on the reason of the prohibition rather than its letter; and note the peculiar hatred carried by the word uncircumcised.

Hold that Samson himself knew the marriage was of the Lord, his desire arising not from carnal affection — she was not the fairer of the two sisters — but from the Spirit urging him toward the occasion it would give against the Philistines, which he concealed from his parents; and set out the rival solutions to the difficulty that others go up to the town where he goes down.

Deny that the case is exemplary at all: Samson was himself a riddle and a paradox, doing what was great and good by what seemed weak and evil, designed to be no pattern for men who must walk by rule rather than example, but a type of him who knew no sin and was made sin for us.

debates: In what sense a forbidden marriage can be said to be of the Lord.
Whether Samson acted on a divine impulse he understood, or was merely overruled.
Whether the law actually forbade a Philistine marriage, or only reached it by its reason.
Whether liking is a sufficient ground for choosing a spouse.
outliers: Henry alone escapes the difficulty by denying that Samson is a pattern, making him a type instead.
Gill alone credits Samson with knowing the divine purpose, against those who allow only permission.
Ellicott alone illustrates the overruling of God from the opening of the Iliad.
Ellicott alone reports the reading that makes Jehovah the one seeking a quarrel.
Clarke alone likens the sufficiency of a lover's will to the motto on a king's artillery.

5.pericope_label: The lion torn in the vineyards, and the honey found in its carcase

schools.summary: Insist that the feat was not done by natural strength but by the Spirit coming upon him, the might being neither his own nor at his command but attached by God's will to his hair and his Nazarite state; treat the ancient belief that bees breed in dead oxen as support for the narrative, quoting Virgil at length; and reckon the interval before the wedding at about a year, that being the usual space between espousal and marriage.

Collect parallels until the exploit looks heroic rather than impossible — Josephus recalling Hercules, an athlete at Olympus, Arabs, David and Benaiah — and correct the verb to mean pervaded; prove from place-names that lions were then common; answer the objection about the bees by showing that the word means a sun-dried skeleton, which bees do not shun, or else that the body was dried without putrefying; deny that the honey could be taken without breaking the Nazarite vow unless a skeleton is no dead body; and decline to fix the length of the interval.

Exculpate Samson over the honey, since on Josephus's account he took pieces of the comb and ate as he walked without touching the carcase, a defilement a Nazarite had especially to avoid; supply a year for the betrothal, twelve months being allowed the bride to prepare; and entertain the reading that it was the father who spoke about the woman to her relations.

Allegorise the scene: young people do not consider how they expose themselves to the lion that seeks to devour when they wander from prudent and pious parents, nor what lions lurk in vineyards; and since Christ has conquered that roaring lion, believers like Samson find honey in the carcase.

debates: Whether the killing of the lion is to be explained by supernatural strength or set beside other feats of strong men.
Whether bees would nest in a dead body, and what the word rendered carcase means.
Whether Samson violated his Nazarite vow in taking the honey.
Why he concealed from his parents where the honey came from.
outliers: Clarke and Ellicott put the same passage of Virgil to opposite uses, one as evidence for the story and the other as the vulgar error that must be cleared away.
Ellicott alone argues from the place-names of Palestine that its wild beasts were once common.
Ellicott alone holds that the vow was broken unless a skeleton counts as no dead body, where Gill exculpates him outright.
Keil alone rejects the skeleton reading as too little, on the ground that bees would not hive in bare bones.
Ellicott alone suggests the riddle was already framed and the silence meant to protect it.

10.pericope_label: The wedding feast, the thirty companions, and the riddle of the eater and the sweet

schools.summary: Approve the feast on principle, since a Nazarite need not affect singularity in such a thing, it being no part of religion to go against the innocent usages of the place we live in, and a reproach to religion when its professors are thought covetous and morose; and offer two readings of the thirty companions, preferring the darker, that men jealous of his strength sent them as a guard or as spies.

Take the bride's relations to have supplied the companions, since Samson brought none — which suggests his marriage was unpopular at home — and reject the ancient variant that makes them afraid of him, since it needs an altered text and does not suit the words that follow; gather the parallels for riddles at feasts, from Solomon to the Sphinx, and grant that this riddle was unfair while defending the terms of the wager as generous; and take the word rendered sheets for fine linen worn next the skin.

Describe the Greek custom of enigmas at festivals, with a crown for the solver and a forfeit of water or brine drunk at one draught for the rest; hold that the riddle could not have been solved without knowing the fact behind it, and that it was cast in verse; identify the promised garments with the Arab hayk, in which the easterner wraps himself as a Highlander in his plaid; and report the versions that read bitter for strong.
Observe that the father went down about the business of the woman, that all three went together, and that the honey of the riddle was such as some men lived on.

debates: Who brought the thirty companions, and whether they came to honour Samson or to watch him.
Whether the ancient reading that they feared him can stand.
Whether the riddle was a fair one, and whether the wager attached to it was.
What garments were staked, and whether the second term of the riddle means strong or bitter.
outliers: Henry alone defends conformity to local custom as no breach of religion, and warns against a reputation for moroseness.
Ellicott alone infers from the absence of Samson's own friends that the marriage was unpopular among his countrymen.
Keil and Ellicott independently reject the same Greek variant, on different grounds.
Ellicott alone quotes Shakespeare against the fairness of the riddle, and translates a German folk-riddle of his own accord.
Ellicott alone argues that the stake was generous even though the riddle was not fair.

15.pericope_label: The threat, the weeping wife, and the ploughing with my heifer

schools.summary: Report that the versions read the fourth day for the seventh to remove the difficulty, prefer the rabbinic explanation that the day named is the sabbath, and record the further proposal that the whole affair covered fourteen days; and note that the answer was brought in before sunset, in time to escape the forfeit.

Deny that the two notices of the seventh day conflict, since the woman had pressed him daily out of curiosity before the threat made her urgent; weigh both parties, finding Samson in no favourable light and the Philistines mean, treacherous and brutal, and observing that the threat to burn her was afterwards carried out; qualify the wife's betrayal by the menaces she was under; and refuse the reading that makes the proverb a charge of adultery, there being no sufficient reason for it.

Allow the wife no motive but obliging her paramours, and take the proverb as a direct charge of adultery, supporting it from Theognis, Plautus and Martial, in all of whom ploughing another man's ground is the standing euphemism, and from the Greek and Syriac versions and a rabbinic authority.

debates: How the seventh day of the threat can be reconciled with weeping through the seven days.
Which party in the story is the more blameable.
How far the wife's betrayal is excused by the threat against her life.
Whether the proverb about ploughing accuses her of adultery.
outliers: The versions cut the chronological knot by altering the number, where the commentators harmonise it.
Ellicott alone passes judgment on the Philistines as well as on Samson.
Ellicott alone suggests the secret was told late in the hope that it could not be passed on in time.
Clarke alone builds the charge of adultery on a wall of classical euphemism, and Ellicott alone dismisses it in a sentence.
Keil calls the proverb perfectly clear without saying what it means, in a passage where two others disagree flatly about it.

19.pericope_label: Ashkelon, the wager paid, and the wife given to his companion

schools.summary: Argue from the order of the narrative that revenge was not the motive, since the anger is kindled only after the deed and is directed at the wife rather than the Philistines; or else decline to defend the act at all, since its morality can be judged only from the standpoint of its time; conjecture that a feast supplied the occasion, rich garments not being everyday wear; raise the possibility that the spoil was armour rather than clothing; and lay the decisive blame on the woman's family, who made the breach irreparable when the marriage tie was not yet broken.

Identify the spoil with the garments of the modern eastern wardrobe; suppose the wife preferred the other man and went to him at once, her betrayal proving her husband was not dear to her whatever tears she shed; and close on the secret rather than the marriage — a man who could not keep his own was foolish to expect better of another, and those who complain of betrayed confidences were their own first betrayers, since a secret never let out of one's bosom cannot be betrayed.
Report that the father gave her away with her own consent, both being affronted at being left, and judging her not merely injured but thereby discharged and free to marry another.

debates: Whether the killing at Ashkelon was revenge, and whether it may be judged at all.
What occasion supplied thirty men wearing garments worth taking.
Whether the spoil was clothing or armour.
Who broke the marriage — the husband who left, or the family who gave the bride away.
outliers: Keil alone defends the act by the sequence of the narrative, showing the anger followed rather than prompted the deed.
Ellicott alone refuses the moral question outright, referring it to the standpoint of the time.
Ellicott alone conjectures a festival as the occasion, reasoning from what men would have been wearing.
Ellicott reports a rendering that would revive the charge of adultery he had himself dismissed two verses earlier.
Clarke alone turns the betrayal into a maxim against confiding secrets at all.
